body: The US uses American English spelling (e.g., center, color) and the imperial system (miles, feet, inches). This contrasts with Canada, which uses British English spelling and the metric system.
Generation 2 coverage is rare in the US, making it a good clue for Canada. However, Alaska and Hawaii are exceptions with significant Generation 2 footage.

US road signs are often more wordy than Canadian ones. For instance, US railway crossing signs say 'RAILROAD CROSSING', while Canadian ones often use symbols. This also applies to yellow diamond warning signs.
US speed limit signs say 'SPEED LIMIT' and use miles per hour, often ending in 5. In contrast, Canadian signs say 'MAXIMUM' and use kilometres per hour.
Yellow, pennant-shaped 'NO PASSING ZONE' signs are exclusive to the US.
American yield signs are an inverted triangle with a red border and the word 'YIELD' inside. Canadian yield signs are similar but lack the text.
US one-way signs are typically horizontal black rectangles with a white arrow and the text 'ONE WAY'. A vertical white version is also used in cities. Canadian signs may lack the text.
US parking signs are typically white with red, green, or black text and are often very wordy. Canadian parking signs are similar but tend to use more symbols.
US highway exit signs are large, green, and rectangular with curved corners. Canadian highway signs are similar but usually have squared corners.
Large blue rectangular signs on highways indicate services like food, gas, and lodging at upcoming exits. These are common in both the US and Canada.
US junction signs are rectangular. In Canada, junction signs are diamond-shaped.
White and orange fibre optic cable markers are a strong clue for the US, as they are very rare in Canada.
The common US construction barrel is orange with horizontal white stripes and a black rubber base, used to block traffic lanes.
The US uses yellow center lines (most often double) and white outer lines. On divided highways, the line closest to the median is also yellow.
Rumble strips, which are indentations on the edge of the pavement, are very common on US highways. They are much rarer in Canada.
Mobile homes, also known as 'trailer' homes, are very common in the rural US, especially in the Southeast. They are much less common in Canada.
Baptist churches are very common throughout the US, particularly in the Southeast and Southern Plains. They are rare in Canada.
Certain gas station and convenience store chains are exclusive to the US and can be a strong clue against Canada.
Many popular US restaurant chains do not operate in Canada, making them a useful country-specific clue.
Both the US and Canada commonly use traffic lights hanging from long horizontal bars over intersections.
North American signposts are often thin metal poles with a U-shaped profile or a series of small holes.
North America predominantly uses wooden utility poles, which can help distinguish it from many parts of Europe where concrete poles are more common.
Insulators that are raised slightly on top of utility poles are a good clue for the US and Canada, as this style is not common in Europe.
The classic North American mailbox sits on a post and has a small side flag.
North American semi-trucks have a long nose because the engine is in front of the cab. This is different from the flat-fronted 'cabover' trucks common in Europe and Asia.
Water towers are common in the US and Canada and often display the town and state name, which can be useful for region-guessing.
US and Canadian Generation 3 coverage usually has no visible antenna, unlike most of Europe. A key exception is in US national parks, where a car with a stubby antenna can be found.
Both the US and Canada have Generation 4 "smallcam" coverage, which is a lower-mounted camera with a large circular blur. Sometimes a car mirror is visible on the right.
The US population is much denser east of the Missouri River compared to the west.
The US uses short licence plates, and each state has a unique design. About half the states do not require front plates, which can be a helpful clue.

Even-numbered Interstates run east-west and increase from south to north, while odd-numbered Interstates run north-south and increase from west to east. US Highways generally follow the opposite numbering pattern.
US phone numbers begin with a three-digit area code that can help identify the region.
Each US state has its own state flag, which are worth learning for region-guessing.
The US has significant elevation in the west with large mountain ranges and high plateaus. The east is generally lower, with the Appalachian Mountains being the most prominent feature.
Eastern and Northern US regions generally have much denser forests than the Western and Southwestern regions.
Corn fields are most common in the Midwest and other specific regions shown on the map.
Soybeans are short, dark green crops found in the Eastern Plains, Midwest, and Lower Mississippi Valley.
Fields of yellow canola flowers are a common sight in North Dakota near the Canadian border.
Cotton, which creates fields of fluffy white flowers, is primarily grown in the Southeast, Lower Mississippi Valley, and parts of Texas, California, and Arizona.
Rice production is limited to north-central California and the Lower Mississippi River Valley, making it a great clue for region-guessing.
Oil pumpjacks are most common in western states like Texas, New Mexico, and North Dakota.
The Great Plains are a vast, mostly flat and treeless region in the middle of the US, stretching from Canada to Texas.
'Prairie potholes', which are wetlands with marshy grasses and shallow ponds, are found from the Montana-Saskatchewan border to the Western Great Lakes.
The Appalachians are low, forested mountains in the eastern US. Architecture differs from north to south, with New England architecture in the north and houses with fewer storeys in the south.
Southern pines, such as the loblolly and longleaf, are tall with fluffy needle clusters and are a key indicator of the southeastern US.
Reddish soil is a common feature of the Deep South, from Oklahoma to South Carolina.
Lawns in the southern US use grasses that turn beige or brown in the winter, unlike the greener winter lawns of the north.
The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.

The Rocky Mountains, stretching from the Canadian border to Northern New Mexico, feature jagged, rocky formations with many pine trees and visible snow year-round at high peaks. Some areas of the range are noticeably dry.

The Great Basin, centered around Nevada, has tall, sometimes snow-capped mountains with dry, grassy, and shrubby plains. The landscape varies with gradual, rocky hills in Oregon and greener mountains in Idaho and central Utah.
Great Basin Sagebrush is a short, shrubby blue-green bush common in arid areas of the interior western United States.
Saguaro cacti, shaped like tall tubes with several branches, are most commonly found in southern Arizona, on the Sonoran border.

Extremely tall conifer trees (Douglas firs) with dark brown bark and dark green leaves are common in Cascadia but can also be found in northern California, Idaho, and Montana. They are also common in British Columbia.
Temperate rainforests with broadleaf trees, large conifers, and ferns are found in coastal Washington, Oregon, and Northern California, extending north into British Columbia and Alaska.
The Southwest, centered around the Four Corners region, features many red-colored mesas and tablelands, along with common red soil.
Palm trees, like the Mexican Fan Palm, are common in the coastal Southeastern states and the Desert Southwest region, including California and the Gulf Coast.
The Texas Hill Country, west of Austin and San Antonio, is an area of dry, rocky hills featuring many yucca and prickly pear plants, with Texas Live Oak trees being predominant.
The Rio Grande Valley in South Texas is extremely flat and features shrubby trees and agricultural fields.
Spanish moss, appearing as greyish-white drapes, can sometimes be seen on trees in the deep south.
Agricultural golden fields are common in eastern Washington and can also appear in flat areas of northern and eastern Oregon.
Central Valley, California has a Mediterranean climate with vineyards and olive trees. Rolling hills can be seen toward the edges of the valley.
The Nebraska Sandhills are a recognizable region of rolling hills covered with prairie grass in the central-north part of the state.
The Appalachian area from southern New York to southern Virginia has many forest-covered rolling hills with flat valleys dividing them. Most ridges are oriented Southwest to Northeast.
The Ouachita Mountains in Eastern Oklahoma and West-Central Arkansas are typically steeper and more visible from a distance than the nearby Ozark Mountains.
Maximum speed limits vary by state and territory, with the highest speeds generally found on interstate highways.
Each state has its own unique, recognizable highway shield.
Most states have unique, distinct, and learnable Adopt-a-Highway signs on the side of roads, which are useful for region-guessing.
Blue and yellow shields are used for county roads in certain US states, though some counties may have unique designs.
Rectangular raised pavement markers are found in the south and west of the US and also in Massachusetts.
Snowplowable raised pavement markers, resembling the letter H, are only found on highways in the eastern states shown in the image.
Kentucky uses uniquely-shaped rumble strips that are thin, relatively long recessed lines on the very outside edges of the road.
The Lower Mississippi River Valley is a very flat and open landscape with red soil in areas of Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Northeast Louisiana. Corn and other crops are common in this area.

Infrastructure in US National Parks, like guardrails and signs, is often painted a medium brown. These parks are mostly in the west, and sometimes feature rock walls instead of guardrails.
Wisconsin and Missouri use a lettering system for their county highways. Wisconsin signs typically include the word ‘county’, while Missouri signs usually do not.
Concrete paving on main highways is a very common sight in Iowa. On residential streets, it is more widespread across the Midwest and East Coast.

Yellow center lines with a noticeably large gap between them are most common in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oregon. They can also appear in a few other states, so use with other clues.
Some roads in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland use middle yellow lines that are thicker than normal. This is not on all roads, so use it as a supporting clue.
Speed signs in Oregon often just say ‘Speed’ instead of the standard ‘Speed Limit’.
A black stripe between the two yellow, middle road lines can sometimes be seen in California.
Utility poles in California often have 3 yellow stripes at the bottom.
Some small roads in California have no middle yellow line, featuring only solid white lines on the sides. This can be seen rarely in other states.
This bollard, found in Nevada, consists of a reflector on a thin stick. The reflector is a vertical white rectangle with a black outline.
The most common bollard in South Dakota and Montana is a dark metal post with a white diamond on top. These can also be found in other western states.
Roadside bollards in Wyoming are often dark metal poles with a white circular reflector. The top of the pole is sometimes painted white or grey, which is unique to the state.
Washington uses bollards that are a white or brown post with a white rectangle on the front and two smaller white or silver squares on the back.
Streets in Utah and Idaho are often named with a number and cardinal direction (e.g., ‘600 South’), especially in urban areas. This can rarely be seen in other Western states.
Texas roads often have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’ road surface. Similar pavement can be seen in adjacent states.
Rural roads in the Upper Midwest, especially Illinois, can have a grainy, ‘salt and pepper’ road surface similar to Texas, though the color may vary.
Yellow or red bands around signposts are a common sight in Texas. Similar reflectors can sometimes be seen in other states.
These white reflectors on signposts are unique to Kansas, most commonly seen on rural ‘stop’ signs.
In Minnesota, yellow signs with vertical, black triangles are placed before bridges and at the ends of guardrails on large highways.
Most rural ‘stop’ signposts in Minnesota have a black-and-white marker attached horizontally to the post.
These green ATV Route signs are unique to Wisconsin.
A rectangular white metal plate with an orange rectangle and diamond can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.
These simple white bollards with black reflectors are unique to Wisconsin.

In Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula, you can often find horizontal blue, red, or green driveway signs that include the house number and often the town or road name. Similar signs in nearby states usually only have numbers.
Signs attached to two signposts are a common, though not exclusive, feature in Michigan.

Many large intersections in Michigan have stop lights and signs that hang from wires across the middle of the intersection, often in yellow boxes. This is most common in Michigan, but not entirely unique.

In rural and exurban Ohio, Lower Michigan, and Indiana, properties often have a vertical metal sign (usually blue or green) with white numbers indicating the house number. These are often attached to mailboxes.
West Virginia sometimes features street signs with a symbol that resembles a fraction inside a circle.

North Carolina commonly uses a style of street signs showing street numbers and arrows in addition to the street name. NOTE: Other states occasionally feature street signs with similar designs, so use other clues before guessing.
In Oklahoma, you can often find a green rectangular sign with 3 rows of numbers attached to the back of stop signs at rural intersections.
Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen attached to signposts at intersections in Pennsylvania. On top, the number of the converging state route is written.
Rectangular white signs can sometimes be seen at intersections in Virginia.
White signs attached to signposts can commonly be seen in North Carolina.
Black street signs with white text can commonly be found at intersections in South Carolina.

Square guardrails are the most dominant type of guardrail in New York and Wyoming. They have a long bar across the top, with several square legs supporting them. These guardrails can be found, to a lesser extent, in some adjacent states.
In New Hampshire there will often be a white metal sign with the characters ‘E-2’ on it adjacent to the road, typically at either end of bridges.
Vermont features small, rectangular green signs on stop sign posts with three rows of numbers. New York uses similar signs, but they can be attached to various post types.
Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts use small green and red rectangular signs to mark the ends of bridges and guardrails.
In rural areas of Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire, short rock walls are commonly visible adjacent to the road. These can be found rarely in adjacent states.
Dark-coloured wooden fences with several horizontal wooden supports are common in farming areas of central and southern Appalachia, from Pennsylvania to Georgia.
Stilt houses can sometimes be seen on the coast. These are especially common toward the south, and on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
Similar to stilt houses, houses with much shorter stilts (1-3 feet) are common in the western and central Gulf Coast, primarily near the coast and rivers.
Buildings with very large, sloped roofs are most common in Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana.
Houses in coastal New England often feature shingle walls, which are layered, overlapping wood panels.

Older three-story wooden houses, or ‘stacked triplexes,’ are very common in urban areas of the Northeast, especially New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. They are also common in Atlantic Canada.
Brownstone buildings are row houses or government buildings made of brick and sandstone, most common in dense urban areas of the Northeast US and Chicago.
Buildings with red metal rooftops are most common in the Mid-South and Southern Appalachia states like Virginia, West Virginia, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, and North Carolina.
Very narrow, one-storey wooden houses called ‘shotgun houses’ are most common in and around New Orleans (LA), Houston (TX), Louisville (KY), and Mississippi.
Pueblo Revival style houses, made of adobe or brick with rounded edges and flat roofs, are commonly seen in New Mexico, and to a lesser extent in Arizona and Colorado.

Spanish Colonial Revival architecture features lightly-coloured stucco walls and red clay-tile roofs. They are found in the desert southwest states of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Texas, as well as Florida and coastal Georgia.
Houses and commercial buildings in the interior Western US are often made of dark wooden boards and timbers. Buildings at high elevations also commonly have metal roofs to avoid snow build-up.
‘Shoprite’ is a regional supermarket chain in 6 states in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic: Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and Maryland.
‘Hy-Vee’ is a supermarket common primarily in the Upper Midwest states of Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Illinois.
The supermarket chain ‘Piggly Wiggly’ is found mostly in the Southeast, as well as Wisconsin.
‘H-E-B’ is a supermarket that is only located in Texas, with most stores in large cities.
‘Publix’ is a regional supermarket chain primarily in Florida and adjacent areas of the Deep South.
‘Waffle House’ is a restaurant chain primarily found in the Southern and Southeast US, with Georgia having the most locations.
‘Carl’s Jr.’ and ‘Hardee’s’ are related fast-food restaurants. Carl’s Jr. is on the West Coast and Southwest, while Hardee’s is in the central and Eastern US. Wyoming and Oklahoma have both.
‘Zaxby’s,’ a fast-food chicken chain, is most common in the Southeast US, especially Georgia. There are also pockets of locations in states like Utah and Montana.
‘Whataburger’ is a hamburger restaurant with locations across the South Central US, with Texas having the most locations by far.
‘Pizza Ranch’ is a restaurant chain found in the middle of the country, with Iowa and Minnesota having the most locations.
‘Tim Hortons’, while Canadian, has many US locations, primarily in states adjacent to Ontario and Quebec, with a few in Texas and Georgia.
‘In-N-Out Burger’ is a regional fast-food chain located primarily in the Southwest US, with California having the most locations.
‘WaWa’ is a regional gas station and convenience store chain in the Mid-Atlantic states and Florida, with the highest density in New Jersey and the Philadelphia area.
The regional gas station ‘Sheetz’ is located in the Eastern US, primarily in the Mid-Atlantic and Central Appalachian areas, with the most stores in Pennsylvania.
‘Kwik Trip’ is a gas station chain in Wisconsin and Minnesota. In Iowa, they are called ‘Kwik Star’.
‘Casey’s’ is a gas station chain found in the Midwest, Plains, and parts of the Mid-South, with the most locations in Illinois, Iowa, and Missouri.
‘Kum & Go’ is a gas station chain based in Iowa, with other locations in the Ozarks, Colorado, Wyoming, and North Dakota.
‘Buc-ee’s’ is a chain of massive gas stations primarily in Texas, known for their huge convenience stores and numerous gas pumps.
Alaska is the largest, northernmost, westernmost, and easternmost US state. A separate guide is available.
Hawaii is the youngest state and the only one outside North America. A separate guide is available.
Puerto Rico is a US territory in the Caribbean. A separate guide is available.
American Samoa is a US territory in the South Pacific. A separate guide is available.
Guam is a US territory and the largest island in Micronesia. A separate guide is available.
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth in the Northwest Pacific. A separate guide is available.
The United States Virgin Islands is a US territory in the Caribbean and is the only part of the US where people drive on the left. A separate guide is available.
The US Minor Outlying Islands are several small US territories, with Midway Atoll being the most relevant for Geoguessr. A separate guide is available.
Interstate 19 in Arizona is the only US highway that uses kilometres for distance and exit signs, though speed limits are still in MPH.
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania is recognizable by its many bright yellow steel bridges, its location at the confluence of 3 rivers, and the surrounding steep bluffs.
San Francisco features Victorian-style row houses with bay windows and ornate details. The houses are often colourful and built close together.
New Orleans is known for its colourful shotgun-style houses and buildings with second-story wrap-around balconies.
Historic areas of Miami and Miami Beach are known for their multi-story Art Deco buildings, often painted in bright colours and located near the coast.
Dry Tortugas National Park is identifiable by a hexagonal brick fort with a moat. Nearby Loggerhead Key has a lighthouse with a brown top and white bottom.
The Florida Keys are tropical islands connected by a highway with lush vegetation and sandy white soil.
The area of South Florida between Fort Myers and Miami has dense, jungle-like forests and long, straight roads.
The only hilly area in central or southern Florida is between Orlando and Lakeland, featuring low, rolling hills, lakes, and agriculture.
Southwestern Oklahoma has a small area of rocky, shrubby peaks, with some trees and rocks that can have a pinkish-red tint.
Central Colorado has a large north-to-south mountain ridge separating the Rockies from the Great Plains, adjacent to Denver, Boulder, and Colorado Springs.
Big Bend National Park in Southwest Texas features dry, rocky peaks and desert plants like yucca and prickly pear cacti.
The Guadalupe Mountains are a ridge of tall, dry peaks on the New Mexico-Texas border, with smaller, flat-topped foothills nearby.
Death Valley National Park is recognized by its dry, sandy, treeless mountains and a dusty sky in Generation 3 coverage.
Glacier National Park in Montana features extremely tall, steep mountain peaks, often with hazy summer coverage.
Badlands National Park is known for its distinct sand-brown, eroded rock formations.
Theodore Roosevelt National Park has sand-brown, eroded rock formations similar to the Badlands, but with more trees and visible fall colours.
Devil’s Tower in Northeastern Wyoming is a very tall, standalone butte visible from miles away.
The Black Hills of South Dakota and Wyoming are mountains with many conifer trees and rocky outcroppings, surrounded by flatter land.
